finding: Test 19's positive half asserts that the `--role` instruction 'still names the spec path and the convergence statement', and §4.2.3 says it 'keeps the round's convergence statement and the path to the spec'. Measured on the freshly built binary against this spec at round 7: the convergence statement is not in `review_loop.instruction` at all. It is the sibling key `review_loop.convergence` — 'no convergence-blocking finding survives verification in 2 consecutive rounds (critical or high severity under review_converge_on=blocking, any severity under all)'. `instruction` is six sentences and none of them is that: (1) 'For each prompt, spawn a sub-agent via the Agent tool.' (2) 'Merge findings (tp review --merge), verify and resolve them, then record the round: tp review spec/0.36.0.md --record <findings.ndjson>.' (3) 'Repeat until tp review spec/0.36.0.md --status --check exits 0.' (4) 'Read the spec at <abs path> before processing each prompt.' (5) 'Process the regression prompt first and apply its findings before or together with the three role prompts.' (6) 'Between counted rounds, you may run tp review spec/0.36.0.md --perspective regression alone as an uncounted delta pass.' An engineer implementing test 19 as written writes an assertion that fails on every correct build. And the rule the test is derived from is not exhaustive: §4.2.3 rules on two of the six sentences (1 and 5, both dropped) and names two retentions, one of which lives in another key — leaving four sentences unruled, of which (2), (3) and (6) are as unfollowable by a single-prompt unit as the two that are dropped, since a unit does not merge, does not record the round and does not run delta passes. The emitted string under `--role` is therefore not pinned: two engineers produce materially different text and both satisfy test 19.
suggestion: Quote the emitted instruction in §4.2.3 and mark every sentence keep or drop, the way §2.2 and §3.2 fix their clauses verbatim, then have test 19 assert byte equality against that quoted text instead of a two-negatives-plus-two-positives predicate. Remove 'the convergence statement' from the retention list — it is `review_loop.convergence`, which `--role` does not touch — or state explicitly that the sibling key is unchanged and give test 19 that assertion instead.

finding: Test 19's second half — "Without `--role`, it is byte-identical to v0.35.2's" — reinstates exactly the cross-version baseline §6.1 abolishes three subsections earlier. §6.1 is titled 'Two conditions every test below runs under' and states: 'There is no cross-version baseline… a `go test` binary compiles one source tree — the current one — so the old emitter is not callable from the new one', written about tests 5 and 12 comparing against 'the v0.35.2 payload'. Test 19 is new in this round's §6.4 and makes the same comparison against the same version. It is worse placed than the two §6.1 repaired, because the artifact it compares is machine- and spec-dependent: measured on the freshly built binary at round 7, `review_loop.instruction` embeds this machine's ABSOLUTE path ('Read the spec at /Users/deligoez/Developer/deligoez/projects/tp/spec/0.36.0.md before processing each prompt') plus the spec's own filename three more times. So a committed literal encodes one checkout and one spec, and obtaining the string by running the old emitter is precisely what §6.1 rules out. Half of the release's only guard on the key §4.2.3 changes has no obtainable baseline, and the failure is the one §6.1 exists to prevent, recommitted in the section §6.1 governs.
suggestion: Delete the v0.35.2 reference and restate test 19's negative half as a property of the current tree, the way §6.1 does for tests 5 and 12: assert the sentence-level predicate on this build — without `--role` the emitted `review_loop.instruction` contains the spawn-a-sub-agent sentence and the regression-ordering sentence; with `--role` it contains neither — with both sides obtained from the same invocation pair. Add one line to §6.1 saying its no-cross-version rule governs §6.4 as well as §6.2 and §6.3, since test 19 shows 'every test below' is not being read that way.

finding: §4.1's table labels 131,727 B 'Payload' and every downstream figure — §4.3's 526,908 / 49,567 / 90.6% — is derived from it, but the number is the sum of the prompt bodies, not the payload. Its own rows prove it: 49,567 + 82,160 = 131,727 exactly, leaving no room for any JSON structure. Re-measured on the current binary at round 7 of this spec: the raw piped payload is 181,119 B while the five prompt bodies sum to 171,791 B, so 9,328 B (5.4%) of what a unit actually parses is uncounted. What matters for §4's claim is that 5,372 B of that is fixed per invocation (`structured_elements` 2,650 B, `review_loop` 918 B, plus `spec`/`spec_ref`/`spec_path`/`skipped_roles`) and `--role` removes none of it — every one of the N units still receives all of it. At N=4 that is ~21.5 KB the flag cannot reach, roughly 43% of the 49,567 B §4.3 books as the post-flag total, putting the real reduction nearer 87–88% than 90.6%. This is a different term from round 6's decomposition of the saved bytes into a regression share and an (N-1)/N share: that was about how the saving splits, this is about what the measured quantity is.
suggestion: Relabel the column 'Prompt bytes' and add the payload's fixed remainder as its own row, stated with the round it was measured on per §4.1's own rule. Then restate §4.3 as 'X emitted bytes down to (own prompt + N × fixed remainder)' so the floor `--role` cannot go below is visible to a reader deciding whether the flag is earned. Also worth naming as the next real saving: `structured_elements` is the largest fixed term and the emitted prompt already restates all of it as its 'Check each of these specifically' list, so a `--role` caller parses that inventory twice — either say what a single-role unit does with the top-level copy, or record that dropping it is where the remaining bytes are.

finding: §4.2.3 rests a deliberate omission on a prohibition Non-Goal 7 does not contain, and the reading that would make the citation true condemns §4.2.3's own change. §4.2.3: 'It does not reword the unrestricted instruction — the sentence naming "the three role prompts" is stale against a four-role corpus, but that is a pre-existing defect and fixing it here would change what every non---role caller reads, which Non-Goal 7 forbids.' Non-Goal 7 reads: 'Changing what a round asks. The checklist items, role rules and output schema are untouched. The prompt does gain two behavioural clauses — that is §2 and §3, and §1 prices them.' review_loop.instruction's wording is not a checklist item, not a role rule and not the output schema, so on the literal text Non-Goal 7 forbids nothing here. On the broad reading needed to make the citation true — 'what a round asks' means anything the caller reads — §4.2.3's own rewrite of the same key under --role is the violation, since it changes what a --role caller reads. Non-Goal 7's enumeration compounds it: it lists the release's additions to what a caller reads as exactly 'two behavioural clauses — that is §2 and §3', and this release now also changes review_loop.instruction, which §4.2.3 argues is necessary to avoid 'a release breaking a shipped contract it never mentions'.
suggestion: Extend Non-Goal 7 to state what it actually claims — that the checklist items, role rules and output schema are untouched, that the prompt gains §2's and §3's clauses, and that review_loop.instruction's text differs under --role and only under --role — and then have §4.2.3 justify leaving the unrestricted wording alone on its own ground (it is a pre-existing defect out of this release's scope) rather than by citing a Non-Goal.

finding: §4.2.3 specifies the `--role` form of `review_loop.instruction` as a subtraction of two named sentences ("it drops the spawn-a-sub-agent sentence and the regression-ordering sentence, and keeps the round's convergence statement and the path to the spec"), but the string is assembled from six fragments and four of them are unruled. `buildReviewLoopInstruction` (internal/cli/review.go:1941-1954) on the default path emits, in order: (1) "For each prompt, spawn a sub-agent via the Agent tool." (2) "Merge findings (tp review --merge), verify and resolve them, then record the round: tp review <spec> --record <findings.ndjson>." (3) "Repeat until tp review <spec> --status --check exits 0." (4) " Read the spec at <abs> before processing each prompt." then, when regression is included (:1948-1950), TWO sentences, not one: (5) "Process the regression prompt first and apply its findings before or together with the three role prompts." and (6) " Between counted rounds, you may run tp review <spec> --perspective regression alone as an uncounted delta pass." — plus a seventh when `workflow.checks` is registered (:1952-1953): "If any mechanical check failed, fix those failures before spawning sub-agents." §4.2.3 removes (1) and (5) only. Under a literal reading a single-prompt unit is still told to merge the round, record it with `--record`, run an uncounted delta pass, and fix mechanical-check failures before spawning sub-agents — all orchestrator actions, which is precisely the defect ("tells it to do three things it cannot do") §4.2.3 exists to fix. Test 19 asserts only the absence of the two named sentences, so an implementation that leaves the other five in place passes every test in §6.
suggestion: Give the disposition of every fragment the function can emit, not two of them: state which of the seven survive under `--role` (plausibly only (3) and (4)), or state the `--role` instruction as its own whole string. Then have test 19 assert the whole value rather than two absences, so an implementation that drops two sentences and keeps five orchestrator instructions fails.

finding: §4.2.3's new rule keeps `review_loop.instruction` under `--role` and specifies a second variant of its text, but the variant is bytes with no decision behind it and it still leaves three orchestrator-only sentences in a unit's payload. Measured on this spec's round-7 emission, the key's six sentences are: (1) spawn a sub-agent per prompt; (2) merge, verify and resolve, then `tp review <spec> --record <file>`; (3) repeat until `--status --check` exits 0; (4) read the spec at <abs path>; (5) process the regression prompt first; (6) between counted rounds run `--perspective regression` as an uncounted delta pass. §4.2.3 drops only (1) and (5). Sentences (2), (3) and (6) are equally unfollowable by a single-prompt unit, and (2) is actively destructive: a unit that obeyed it would record the round and advance the loop it is a member of. Meanwhile the two things §4.2.3 gives as the reason to keep the key are already on the same payload as their own keys — the convergence statement is the sibling key `review_loop.convergence`, not part of `instruction`, and the spec path is the top-level `spec_path`, which the prompt body then restates a third time as 'Read the spec file before reviewing'. So the variant retains only duplicates and removes only half of what makes the key wrong.
suggestion: Omit `review_loop.instruction` entirely when `prompts[]` has been reduced by `--role`. That costs zero bytes instead of a second maintained string, removes all four orchestrator-only sentences rather than two, and gives §6.3 test 19 a sharper pair of directions (key absent under `--role`; byte-identical without it) than 'reworded variant vs original'. If the key must survive, enumerate the sentences it keeps rather than the two it drops, and state why (2), (3) and (6) are safe for a unit to read.

finding: §4.2.3's repair of review_loop.instruction removes two of the key's orchestrator-only sentences and leaves at least three more, including two that name modes §4.2.2 refuses to a --role caller. The rule is: 'it drops the spawn-a-sub-agent sentence and the regression-ordering sentence, and keeps the round's convergence statement and the path to the spec.' Read against the emitter (internal/cli/review.go buildReviewLoopInstruction, lines 1941-1954) the key is assembled from four pieces, not two. The first is a single fmt.Sprintf literal containing three sentences — 'For each prompt, spawn a sub-agent via the Agent tool. Merge findings (tp review --merge), verify and resolve them, then record the round: tp review <spec> --record <findings.ndjson>. Repeat until tp review <spec> --status --check exits 0.' — so dropping 'the spawn-a-sub-agent sentence' still tells a unit to merge, to record the round and to loop until convergence, and --merge, --record and --status are three of the seven modes §4.2.2 refuses to a --role caller outright. The regression block appends two sentences, not one; dropping 'the regression-ordering sentence' leaves 'Between counted rounds, you may run tp review <spec> --perspective regression alone as an uncounted delta pass.' And when the workflow registers checks — as this repository's does — a fourth piece is appended: 'If any mechanical check failed, fix those failures before spawning sub-agents.' §4.2.3's own diagnosis is that the unrestricted key 'tells it to do three things it cannot do'; after the specified repair it still does. §6.4 test 19 asserts only the absence of the two named sentences, so it passes on every one of these.
suggestion: Specify the --role instruction positively rather than as two deletions: give the exact sentences the key carries under --role (the spec path, and whatever single statement of the unit's own obligation is wanted), so anything the emitter appends for the orchestrator is excluded by construction rather than by an enumeration that has to track four append sites. Then have test 19 assert that string, and assert that no --role instruction contains the substrings '--merge', '--record', '--status' or 'sub-agent'.

finding: §6.1 removes `--no-state` and replaces it with two mechanisms offered as a free choice — "a temporary state directory, or a copy of the tree" — and the first one does not exist in tp. `engine.ReviewStateDir` (internal/engine/reviewstate.go:102-106) computes the location as `filepath.Dir(specPath)/.tp-review/<base>`; it takes no override, and no flag or `TP_*` variable anywhere in the tree relocates it. The only way to move review state is to move the spec, so the sentence names one mechanism and a phrase for the same mechanism. Worse, the two readings of that phrase are not equivalent for the release gate. A spec copied alone into a temp directory arrives with no `.tp-review/`, so it is at round 1 for every spec, and `regression` is skipped `no-baseline` (internal/cli/review.go:907-909) across the board. That erases exactly the property §7 buys repository breadth for: "22 version specs ... 15 with recorded rounds and 7 with none — so the corpus exercises both sides of the one skip reason that is round-dependent (`regression`, skipped `no-baseline` at round 1 and emitted after)". Copying the tree *including* `spec/.tp-review/` preserves it; a fresh state directory does not. §6.1 declares the mechanism the implementer's free choice while §7's only gate silently depends on which one is chosen.
suggestion: Fix the mechanism rather than only the outcome, in the one place the outcome is not sufficient: require the isolated tree to carry each spec's existing `spec/.tp-review/<base>/` contents, because the recorded rounds are an input to the panel §6.3 test 14 compares. Drop 'a temporary state directory' as a separate option, or say explicitly that it is legal for §6.2's tests and illegal for tests 13-14.

finding: §6.1's normative property requires "the same prompt without the clauses" and then asserts "Both sides of that equality are obtainable from the current tree — how is a task's decision", immediately after deleting the only construction any draft has offered for the second side, on the ground that it "buys a production toggle whose only false caller is a test". §2.3 makes the append unconditional for every prompt with a non-empty `output_path`, so the current tree emits no such prompt: the second side is not obtainable by running anything. The one construction that needs no new seam is to emit once and strip the known 468-byte suffix — and that makes tests 5 and 12 assert `X == strip(X) + suffix`, an identity that holds for any suffix of any length, passes on a prompt where the clauses are misspelled, reordered or the trailing-newline strip is missing, and cannot fail. So §6.1 leaves an implementer with exactly two options, and rules against one of them without ruling for the other: build the seam §6.1 forbids, or write the release's only byte-cost assertions in a form that could never have failed. That is the outcome CLAUDE.md's evidence rule names — a test that has never been observed failing proves nothing — reached by the section written to prevent it.
suggestion: Name the seam and accept its cost, or drop the equality. An unexported builder parameter (or a builder split into assemble-body / append-clauses, with the test calling the first) has one false caller and is inspectable; it is cheaper than an assertion that cannot refute. If the seam is unacceptable, replace tests 5 and 12 with a direct assertion on the emitted bytes — the body ends with the exact 468-byte suffix (test 3 already does this) and the byte immediately before it is not LF — which is falsifiable without a second side.

finding: Test 18 is a numbered member of the suite and asserts a property of the suite it belongs to: '`spec/.tp-review/` and `.tp/rounds/` under the repository root hash identically before and after the whole suite runs.' No test function can observe that. A Go test sees the tree only at its own execution point and package test order is the harness's, so one engineer writes a `TestMain` wrapper — which is not a numbered test and cannot be reported as 'test 18 passed', the exact defect numbering it was meant to cure — while another writes an ordinary test that hashes twice in succession and passes unconditionally. Independently, the assertion is now vacuous by construction. §6.1 no longer offers a free choice of mechanism: it requires that isolation 'preserve state behaviour and only relocate it — a temporary state directory, or a copy of the tree'. Once that is done no test in the suite touches the repository root, so the two hashes are equal for a reason unrelated to what test 18 measures. It can only fail against an implementation that ignored §6.1 — and against that implementation the 'before' hash was already taken after other tests had written. So on the conforming build it cannot fail, and on the non-conforming build it observes the wrong instant.
suggestion: Make test 18 a property of the isolation seam, which one test can observe: assert that every `tp review`/`tp audit`/`tp run --dry-run` invocation the suite makes resolves its state root to a path under the test's temporary directory rather than the repository root. Keep the before/after directory hash if wanted, but say it is a `TestMain`-level guard, not a numbered test, and define the comparison operationally — the recursive map of relative path to sha256 of file contents, with a directory that does not exist equal to the empty map — so 'hash identically' does not leave mtimes, ordering and create-then-delete undecided.

finding: §6.1 and §6.4 test 19 were both written this round and they contradict each other on the one point §6.1 exists to settle. §6.1 is headed 'Two conditions every test below runs under' and states, as a whole subsection, 'There is no cross-version baseline' — 'Earlier drafts had tests 5 and 12 compare against "the v0.35.2 payload, obtained by running the v0.35.2 emitter in-process". That is not buildable: a go test binary compiles one source tree — the current one — so the old emitter is not callable from the new one.' Test 12 was duly repaired and now says '§6.1's property, not a cross-version comparison'. Test 19, four items later and below the same heading, says: 'Without --role, it is byte-identical to v0.35.2's.' That is the exact comparison §6.1 declares unbuildable, against the exact version it names, and §6.1's scope ('every test below') covers test 19. So the release's newest test is unimplementable by its own spec's finding, and the repair applied to tests 5 and 12 did not propagate to the test added in the same edit.
suggestion: State test 19's without---role half as a property of the current tree, the way test 12 now is: 'Without --role, review_loop.instruction is byte-identical to the same tree's instruction for the same invocation with the flag removed' — obtainable from one source tree, and still the pair that distinguishes 'addressed the single prompt' from 'stopped emitting the key'. Delete the v0.35.2 reference.

finding: §7's argument for gating on repository breadth rests on a claim about regression that §4.1 of this same spec measures the counterexample to. §7: 'the corpus exercises both sides of the one skip reason that is round-dependent (regression, skipped no-baseline at round 1 and emitted after)'. Regression is not emitted merely by being past round 1. §4.1's own table records 'Round 3 (spec unchanged at emission, nothing resolved): 4 prompts' — past round 1, no regression. The emitter agrees: buildReviewPrompts appends regression only under `!noState && round >= 2` AND `diffBlock != "" || len(fixed) > 0` (internal/cli/review.go:871-883), and the no-baseline entry is written to skipped_roles only when `round < 2` (line 907), so at round >= 2 without a diff or a fixed finding regression appears in neither prompts[] nor skipped_roles at all. A gate that iterates the repository's specs read-only emits each at its recorded round with the spec unchanged since that round and nothing newly resolved — the round-3 shape — so it can land on the not-emitted side for every spec and never exercise the emitted side. Breadth does not buy 'both sides'; the emitted side needs a fixture with a diff or a resolved finding, exactly like the four reasons §7 concedes must be built.
suggestion: Correct §7's premise to what the emitter does: regression is emitted only when the round is >= 2 and the spec changed or a finding was resolved fixed, so the corpus supplies the not-emitted side (round 1 and unchanged later rounds) and the emitted side must be supplied by a fixture. Either add that fixture to §6.3 test 9's list, or restate what breadth buys as the section's second sentence already does — 'section structures no fixture author would think to write' — and drop the both-sides claim.

finding: On the tp run path the unit receives two write rules from this release's own artifacts and they disagree, and §2.4 decides not to reconcile them. §2.2's clause, emitted into every role prompt, says 'Read anything, and run tp itself freely — its own state writes are expected. Write no other file except the output file this prompt names.' The shipped agents/tp-reviewer.md — the definition §2.1's table makes load-bearing as the fence for that same path — tells the same agent: 'You may write exactly one file: your own findings file at $TP_ROUND_DIR/role-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson.part ... Every other write is refused — another role's file, another round, the merged file, the spec, the source.' §2.2 reconciles its carve-out with the hook ('a state write performed inside a tp subprocess is not [a tool call]') but never with the definition's prose, which is stated absolutely and which §2.4 explicitly declines to touch ('the definitions are the cheaper channel ... A future release ... should move the clause there and delete it here'). A unit that reads both is told both that running tp freely is expected and that every write beyond one file is refused, and nothing in the release says which governs.
suggestion: Either add one sentence to §2.4 stating that agents/tp-reviewer.md's 'every other write is refused' is a statement about tool calls and that tp's own subprocess state writes are outside it — and make updating that definition's wording part of this release, since it is a one-line prose change and not new surface — or drop 'run tp itself freely' from §2.2's clause and route the carve-out through the definition, where the fence it qualifies actually lives.

finding: The positive half of §4.2.3's rule, and of the test that pins it, names content that is not in the key being edited. §4.2.3: under --role the instruction 'keeps the round's convergence statement and the path to the spec'; §6.4 test 19: 'still names the spec path and the convergence statement.' The convergence statement is not part of review_loop.instruction — it is the sibling key review_loop.convergence, returned separately by the same function (internal/cli/review.go:1931 and 1940, `return convergence, instruction`) and emitted as review_loop.convergence. This round's own emitted payload carries them as two keys. So 'keeps the convergence statement' is vacuous for instruction (it was never there) and trivially true for convergence (which --role does not touch), and test 19's presence assertion has no unambiguous subject: an implementer can satisfy it either by leaving the sibling key alone or by retaining 'Repeat until tp review <spec> --status --check exits 0' — which is itself one of the orchestrator-only sentences the same rule is trying to remove.
suggestion: Drop 'the convergence statement' from both §4.2.3 and test 19, or name it as the sibling key: 'review_loop.convergence is unchanged under --role; only review_loop.instruction differs.' Either way the retained content of instruction should be enumerated by its own words rather than by a phrase that resolves to a different key.

finding: §4.2.3 specifies the `--role` instruction as an edit to a quoted string, and `review_loop.instruction` has four mutually exclusive constructions, not one. In `buildReviewLoopInstruction` (internal/cli/review.go:1919-1946) the value is set at :1919 (default), :1921 (round<2 with prior findings) or :1923 (round>=2), and then unconditionally overwritten at :1941 whenever `--no-state` is absent. The sentence §4.2.3 quotes and removes — "For each prompt, spawn a sub-agent via the Agent tool" — is the :1941 wording; under `--no-state` at round>=2 the string reads "Spawn sub-agents for each prompt." instead, and under `--no-state` it also gains "Convergence is not being recorded (--no-state)." (:1934). A subtractive rule keyed on the quoted sentence silently no-ops on that branch, leaving a `--role` unit with panel-shaped text. Neither §4.2.3 nor test 19 names a round or a state mode, and `--no-state` is a global flag rather than one of the modes §4.2.2's table partitions, so `--role --no-state` is legal and untested. Separately, "keeps the round's convergence statement" is not locatable: `convergence` is a sibling top-level key built at :1931/:1940, not text inside `instruction`; the nearest thing inside `instruction` is "Repeat until tp review <spec> --status --check exits 0."
suggestion: State the rule over the value rather than over one branch's wording — e.g. 'under `--role`, `instruction` is <exact string>, with <spec> and <abs> interpolated as today' — and say which branches it applies to. Replace 'the round's convergence statement' with the sentence actually meant, since the key of that name is a different field.

finding: §4.3's P2 paragraph books the interactive-path win as 'one invocation per role instead of one invocation plus a split script — more invocations, but no script to write, skip or mis-write'. That counts invocations, and in bytes — the unit this release is measured in everywhere else — it is a loss for the party doing the counting. The split script costs the orchestrator ~0 payload bytes: it pipes the payload to a file and never reads it into context. `--role` invoked N times *by the orchestrator* puts N × (own prompt + the fixed payload remainder) into the orchestrator's own context — measured on this spec at round 7, 4 × ~26 KB ≈ 105 KB where the script cost it nothing. The saving exists only when each *unit* makes its own `--role` invocation, which under `tp run` is exactly what §4.2.3's brief delivers, and which nothing this release changes delivers on the interactive path. So P2's claim holds on the driver path and is inverted on the path the paragraph is about — and P2 is the principle whose whole point is that the N case must not cost more than the 1 case.
suggestion: Say who makes the invocation. Rewrite P2 as: under `tp run` each unit invokes its own `--role`, so the N case needs no new surface; on the interactive path the operator must pass `--role <id>` down to each sub-agent, and an operator who instead runs the N invocations themselves pays N payloads in their own context, which is worse than the script. That makes the interactive benefit visibly contingent on an operator instruction this release does not emit, rather than implying the flag delivers it.

finding:
Tests 1 and 2 scope themselves to both commands ('for `tp review` … and the same for `tp audit`'), and §6.3 test 6 does the same ('`tp audit` likewise'), but tests 3, 4 and 5 name no command at all — and the two readings produce different suites. Test 5 is the sharpest case: the −1 row §1.1 calls 'not optional and not cosmetic' rests on 'measured on this spec's own emission, every role prompt body ends with `
`', a sentence whose scope is unstated. I confirmed it for `tp review` only (five role prompts at round 7, every body ending `
`); I could not confirm it for `tp audit` without writing the repository's audit state, which §6.1 forbids. If an audit role prompt body does not end `
`, a test 5 written for both commands fails by exactly one byte on a correct build, and a test 5 written for review alone leaves §2.3's whole construction unasserted for half the prompts §2.2 says the clause serves. Test 4 pulls the other way: its derived mode list is 'every value `--perspective` accepts … plus `--verify`', and §4.2.2 records as verified that `tp audit` registers none of those flags — so test 4 is review-only by construction, while §2.3 states the emission predicate ('every prompt whose `output_path` is non-empty, and to no other') for both commands and leaves its negative half untested on the audit side.
suggestion: Give tests 3, 4 and 5 the same explicit scope sentence tests 1 and 2 carry. For test 5, state whether the exact 467 is asserted for `tp audit` too and, if so, widen §1.1's measurement to 'every role prompt body — review and audit — ends with \n', measured rather than assumed, since the entire −1 depends on it. For test 4, say the empty-`output_path` negative is review-only because `tp audit` has no mode that emits such a prompt, or name the audit mode that does.

finding: §7 and §6.3 test 14 name two different iteration sets for the same gate, and §7 is the section that says what the gate buys. §7 grounds the whole breadth argument on a counted corpus: '22 version specs, 5 KB to 79 KB, 15 with recorded rounds and 7 with none'. Test 14, which §7 declares to be the gate, iterates 'every spec in spec/ the repository can emit prompts for'. Counted in this repository: spec/ holds 39 markdown files — the 22 version-numbered ones §7 counts plus 17 more that are also specs or spec artifacts (0.11.0-review.md, 0.12.0-review-rounds.md ... 0.25.0-role-prompt-research.md, and the non-spec 0.33.0-candidates.md, 0.34.0-guard-tests.md, 0.34.0-release-counts.md, 0.35.0-candidates.md). tp emits prompts for any of them, so test 14's phrase selects 39 while §7's argument and its stated properties (the size range, the 15/7 split) describe 22. An implementer following test 14 runs a gate whose cost and coverage §7 has not characterised; one following §7 runs a narrower gate than the numbered test requires.
suggestion: Fix the set in one place and have the other cite it. Since §7's measured properties are the argument, define the gate's corpus there as the version-numbered specs (spec/<major>.<minor>.<patch>.md, 22 today) and have test 14 say 'every spec in §7's corpus' rather than 'every spec in spec/'. If the wider set is wanted, re-derive §7's counts over all 39 so the section's numbers describe the set the gate actually iterates.
